[OBJECTIVES]: To examine the relationship between changes in objectively assessed sleep and global cognitive functioning from inpatient postacute rehabilitation to 6-month follow-up.
[DESIGN]: Secondary analysis of two prospective, longitudinal studies.

key_findings.finding: Direct evidence is present but appears limited to one clearly matching longitudinal cohort: McCrae et al., “Decrease in daytime sleeping is associated with improvement in cognition after hospital discharge in older adults” (J Am Geriatr Soc, 2014; PMID 25093233). This secondary analysis of two prospective longitudinal studies included 192 older adults (mean age 73.8) in VA inpatient post-acute rehabilitation; wrist actigraphy measured daytime sleep over 7 days during rehabilitation and again at 6 months after discharge, with MMSE at both time points. After adjustment for age, education, sex, BMI, depression, pain, and comorbidity, decreased daytime sleep was associated with MMSE improvement (β = −0.01, t(80) = −3.22, P = .002); change in nighttime wakefulness was not a significant predictor. This is an association, not proof that reducing naps causes cognitive improvement.

source_tools.relevance: Full abstract and results for the directly matching post-acute, post-discharge actigraphy/MMSE longitudinal cohort

key_findings.finding: The direct study does not establish an intervention effect or specifically test intentional nap reduction: daytime sleep was observed longitudinally, and the analysis related within-person change to cognitive change. The evidence therefore supports an association between reduced daytime sleeping and better cognitive trajectory after discharge, with possible residual confounding and incomplete follow-up (78% provided at least partial follow-up).

source_tools.relevance: Study design, observational/secondary-analysis nature, follow-up completeness, and adjusted growth-curve result

key_findings.finding: No additional clearly matching study was identified in the searched post-acute, hospital-to-home, delirium-follow-up, actigraphy, and daytime-nap domains. A small post-discharge cohort (N=23; mean age 74) found that changes in subjective sleep quality, daytime dysfunction, and fatigue predicted physical/functional recovery at 4 weeks, but it did not measure cognition or daytime sleeping/naps by actigraphy; it is not direct evidence for the question.

source_tools.relevance: Post-discharge older-adult cohort with sleep and recovery outcomes, showing functional rather than cognitive endpoints

key_findings.finding: Related longitudinal community evidence should not be substituted for post-discharge evidence: in a 5.5-year cohort of adults aged 55+, excessive daytime sleepiness was associated with later MMSE decline among physically robust participants (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.04–2.13), but this was not a hospital-discharge or post-acute-care cohort and did not test decreased naps/daytime sleep as a recovery exposure.

source_tools.relevance: Clearly labeled indirect community longitudinal cohort with daytime sleepiness and cognitive outcome

key_findings.finding: Qualitative delirium follow-up evidence in 10 octogenarians after aortic valve replacement reported persistent sleep disturbance up to 4 years and patient-described struggles between sleep and activity, but it did not quantify daytime naps or test cognition longitudinally; it cannot answer whether decreased daytime sleeping improves cognition.

source_tools.relevance: Delirium-related longitudinal qualitative follow-up, explicitly lacking quantitative cognition/napping association
